title: The Holistic Baby and Toddler Sleep Podcast
author: Georgina Windebank
description: Holistic sleep consultant, naturopath and nutritionist Georgina Windebank shares tips, education and knowledge for solving baby and toddler sleep issues, so parents feel equipped and confident.

episodes.title: Ep 53: 3 most common mistakes parents make with their 3 year old's sleep
episodes.summary: Three-year-olds push back at bedtime and need connection, day sleep, good overnight sleep, nutrition and support with big emotions. Georgina covers the common mistakes around transitions like a new sibling, a big bed, dropping the nap, dropping the dummy and starting kindergarten.

episodes.title: Ep 52: Surviving 2 year old sleep: Why is it so tricky and what actually helps
episodes.summary: Why two-year-old sleep gets hard, from developmental pushback to boundaries, and a step-by-step framework covering nap length, dummy dependence and bedtime stalling.

episodes.title: Ep 51: Living with sleep anxiety and practical tips to manage it
episodes.summary: Georgina shares her own story of anxiety and sleep, with practical tips for parents managing sleep anxiety. Includes content warnings for postpartum depression and loss.

episodes.title: Episode 50: 5 min Express Episode. What is the 1 thing which will help your child's sleep today!
episodes.summary: The single biggest lever for child sleep is preventing overtiredness. Georgina gives six practical tips, promising easier naps, smoother bedtimes, fewer night wakes and less early rising.

episodes.title: Episode 49: Is there ever a time I should wake my sleeping child?
episodes.summary: Georgina challenges the saying "never wake a sleeping baby." Too much day sleep can eat into a child's 24-hour sleep capacity and cause bedtime resistance, night waking and early rising. For parents of babies over four months.

episodes.title: Ep 48: Why is nap placement so important for good child sleep?
episodes.summary: How the timing and length of naps affect sleep quality, ease of settling, feeding and mood, and why nap placement is the foundation for fixing short naps, night waking and early rising.

articles.question: Should you ever wake a sleeping baby?
articles.metaDescription: Sleep consultant Georgina Windebank explains when waking a napping baby actually fixes bedtime battles, night waking and early rising.
articles.intro: Yes, sometimes you should wake a sleeping baby. On The Holistic Baby and Toddler Sleep Podcast, sleep consultant and naturopath Georgina Windebank argues that "never wake a sleeping baby" is simply wrong for babies over about four months. A child can only sleep a certain amount in 24 hours, and when too much of it happens during the day, you pay for it at bedtime, overnight and at 5am.

sections.heading: Sleep is a 24-hour budget
sections.body:
Georgina's core idea is that every child has a sleep capacity for the day, set by their age and their own individual needs. That total gets split between naps and night. If a long afternoon nap takes a bigger share than it should, there's less sleep pressure left for the night, and the night gets shorter or more broken.

This is why the old advice fails. It treats daytime sleep as free, when really it's drawn from the same account as night sleep. A baby who naps for three hours in the afternoon isn't banking extra rest. They're spending tonight's sleep early.

The host explains that this becomes relevant from around four months, once a baby's sleep starts to organise into more predictable cycles and a routine is possible. Before that, newborn sleep is scattered and letting them sleep is usually the right call.

quote.text: A child can only sleep a certain amount (depending on their age and their own sleep needs)
quote.speaker: Georgina Windebank

sections.heading: Three signs your baby is sleeping too much in the day
sections.body:
Georgina lists the problems that too much day sleep produces. If you're seeing one or more of these, an overlong or badly timed nap is the first suspect:

- **Difficulty settling at bedtime.** The baby isn't tired enough because a late or long nap drained the sleep pressure. Bedtime turns into a long fight, and it's not because they're overtired; it's because they're undertired.
- **Night waking.** With the daytime share too big, the night gets fragmented. The baby wakes because they've had enough sleep, not because something's wrong.
- **Early rising.** The 5am wake-up is often a baby who has simply completed their sleep budget early.

Parents commonly respond to all three by adding more sleep, longer naps or an earlier bedtime. Georgina's point is that the fix is often the opposite: cap the nap.

quote.text: Too much day sleep can result in: difficulty settling your child at bedtime
quote.speaker: Georgina Windebank

sections.heading: When waking your baby is the right move
sections.body:
So when do you wake them? Based on the episode, the cases are:

1. **The nap is running past the amount your child needs for their age.** If a baby who needs a certain total of day sleep is blowing past it in one nap, wake them so the rest of the day and the night stay on track.
2. **The nap is drifting too late.** A nap that ends close to bedtime steals from the night. Waking a little earlier protects an age-appropriate bedtime.
3. **You're trying to establish a routine.** For families over the four-month mark who want predictable naps and nights, consistent nap end times are part of building that rhythm.

The host explains that this isn't about being rigid. It's about knowing the optimal nap timing and duration for your child's age and gently steering toward it, which is exactly what her Ultimate Feeding and Sleep Guide lays out.

sections.heading: How to wake a baby without wrecking the afternoon
sections.body:
Waking a baby sounds harsh, but done gently it's uneventful. Open the blinds, let normal household noise in, talk softly and give them a few minutes to surface. Most babies wake happily when their room brightens and the world gets interesting.

Then watch the results over several days rather than judging one night. If bedtime gets easier, night wakes reduce and the early morning start shifts later, the nap was the culprit. If nothing changes, look at the other levers Georgina covers on the show, particularly nap placement and preventing overtiredness, which her related episodes treat as the foundations of good child sleep.

The takeaway is simple: day sleep and night sleep come from the same pot. Sometimes the kindest thing you can do for tonight is to end this afternoon's nap.

keyTakeaways: "Never wake a sleeping baby" is wrong for babies over about four months; day and night sleep share one 24-hour budget.
Too much day sleep shows up as bedtime resistance, night waking and early rising.
Wake your baby when a nap runs past their age-appropriate total or drifts too close to bedtime.
Cap the nap gently with light, sound and a few minutes to wake up.
Judge the change over several days, and then look at nap placement and overtiredness if problems persist.

faq.q: At what age can you start waking a baby from naps?
faq.a: Georgina aims this advice at parents of babies over four months who are establishing a routine or dealing with sleep problems. Newborn sleep is too irregular to manage this way.

faq.q: Why does my baby wake at 5am every day?
faq.a: Early rising is one of the three signs of too much day sleep in the episode. Your baby may simply be finishing their sleep budget early because naps took too large a share.

faq.q: Will waking my baby from a nap make them overtired?
faq.a: Not if the nap has already run long. The episode's point is that these babies are undertired at bedtime, not overtired. Preventing overtiredness is still important, which Georgina covers separately in Episode 50.
